intro:
This unit is built on thirteen ideas from general chemistry and the first third of Organic I. If you hold them, most of the unit can be worked out: which acid is stronger, which chair is lower, which mechanism runs. If one is missing, that part of the unit turns into a list to memorize, and lists are what fail under exam pressure.

The check below has two short questions per idea and takes about twenty minutes. It shows which refreshers to read first, so that study time goes to the gaps and not to what is already solid. A miss here is cheap. The same miss on the exam is not.

axioms.title: A skeletal structure hides hydrogens, lone pairs and formal charges
axioms.statement: Every corner and line end is a carbon with enough hydrogens to make four bonds. Lone pairs are usually not drawn, and formal charge is valence electrons minus lone pair electrons minus bonds.
axioms.why: Every arrow starts from electrons, so electrons you have not counted are electrons you cannot push.
explains: NMR (lecture 10/22): counting signals means seeing every hydrogen, including the ones that are not drawn.
E2 (lecture 11/12): the base removes a β hydrogen that the skeletal drawing does not show.
Chairs (lectures 10/20 and 10/27): every ring carbon has an axial and an equatorial bond, and the undrawn ones hold hydrogens.
Acids and bases (lecture 10/29): the charge on a conjugate base comes from counting its lone pairs.
Exam questions that ask for a mechanism: charges must balance in every step, and they only balance if the hidden atoms are counted.
axioms.refresher:
A skeletal structure is shorthand. Every corner and every line end is a carbon. Carbon makes four bonds, so any bond you do not see is a bond to hydrogen. Atoms other than carbon are written out, together with the hydrogens on them.

[[mol:CCC(C)Br]]

This drawing has four carbons. The two ends of the chain are {{CH3}} groups (three hydrogens each), the corner next to one end is a {{CH2}} (two), and the carbon holding Br has one. That is nine hydrogens: {{C4H9Br}}.

Lone pairs are left out as well. In a neutral molecule nitrogen has one, oxygen has two and a halogen has three.

Formal charge = valence electrons − lone pair electrons − number of bonds.

  • Oxygen in {{CH3O-}}: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.
  • Oxygen in {{H3O+}}: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.
  • Carbon with three bonds and no lone pair: 4 − 0 − 3 = +1, a carbocation.
  • Carbon with three bonds and one lone pair: 4 − 2 − 3 = −1, a carbanion.

Before you draw any arrow, write in the hydrogens and lone pairs around the place where the reaction happens. Most arrow mistakes begin with an atom whose electrons were never counted.

axioms.title: Electronegativity makes bonds polar
axioms.statement: In a bond between different atoms the more electronegative atom takes the larger share of the electrons, so it is electron rich (δ−) and its partner is electron poor (δ+). Electronegativity rises to the right in a row and up a column.
axioms.why: Reactions happen between electron rich and electron poor atoms, so you have to be able to find both.
explains: SN2 (lectures 11/03 and 11/05): the carbon of C-Br is δ+, which is why a nucleophile attacks it.
Organometallics (lectures 10/29 and 11/03): in C-Li and C-Mg the carbon is δ−, so RLi and RMgX act as carbanions.
Acids and bases (lecture 10/29): across a row, the more electronegative atom holds a negative charge better, so {{H2O}} is a stronger acid than {{NH3}}.
Induction (lecture 10/29): the fluorines of {{CF3CO2H}} pull electrons through the bonds and stabilize its conjugate base.
NMR (lecture 10/22): hydrogens near an electronegative atom are in a different electronic environment and give a different signal.
axioms.refresher:
Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons of a bond. The values to know: F 4.0, O 3.5, N 3.0, Cl 3.0, Br 2.8, C 2.5, H 2.1, Mg 1.2, Li 1.0. It rises to the right across a row and up a column of the periodic table.

When two bonded atoms differ, the electrons sit closer to the more electronegative one. That atom is partly negative (δ−) and the other is partly positive (δ+). The bond is polar.

[[mol:CBr]]

In bromomethane, bromine (2.8) beats carbon (2.5). Carbon is δ+, electron poor. Something with electrons to give will go there.

[[mol:C[Li]]]

In methyllithium it is the other way round. Carbon (2.5) beats lithium (1.0) by a wide margin, so carbon is δ−, electron rich, and behaves almost like {{CH3-}}.

C-H bonds are close to nonpolar (2.5 against 2.1), which is why alkanes do so little.

The habit to build: look at each bond to an atom that is not carbon or hydrogen, decide which end is δ+ and which is δ−, and you have found the places where the molecule can react.

axioms.title: Electrons flow from rich to poor, and curved arrows show it
axioms.statement: A nucleophile (a Lewis base) gives an electron pair to an electrophile (a Lewis acid). A curved arrow shows two electrons moving: it starts at a lone pair or a bond and ends at an atom or at a bond.
axioms.why: Every mechanism in this unit is two to four of these arrows, and the exam marks each one.
explains: SN2 (lecture 11/03): one arrow from the nucleophile's lone pair to carbon, one from the C-LG bond to the leaving group.
SN1 and E1 (lecture 11/10): the first arrow starts at the C-LG bond and ends on the leaving group, leaving a carbocation.
E2 (lecture 11/12): three arrows in one step, from the base to H, from the C-H bond to the C-C bond, and from the C-LG bond to the leaving group.
Acid and base reactions (lecture 10/29): a proton transfer is the same two arrows as an SN2, at hydrogen instead of carbon.
Exam questions that say 'draw the mechanism': arrows that start at an atom or at a charge sign lose the points.
axioms.refresher:
A nucleophile has an electron pair it can give: a lone pair, often with a negative charge ({{HO-}}, {{CH3O-}}, {{-CN}}, {{NH3}}). It is a Lewis base. An electrophile can accept a pair: it has a δ+ atom or a positive charge (the carbon of {{CH3Br}}, a carbocation, {{H3O+}}). It is a Lewis acid.

A curved arrow shows one pair of electrons moving.

  • The tail sits on the electrons: a lone pair or a bond. Never on a bare atom, and never on a plus sign.
  • The head points to where the electrons end up: on an atom (as a new lone pair, or as a new bond to that atom) or between two atoms (a new bond).
[[rxn:C[O-] + CBr>>COC + [Br-]]]

Here the first arrow starts at a lone pair on the oxygen of methoxide and ends at the carbon of bromomethane: a new O-C bond. Carbon cannot have five bonds, so a second arrow starts at the C-Br bond and ends on bromine, which leaves with the pair as {{Br-}}.

Check every step two ways. The total charge is the same on both sides. The atom at the tail becomes one unit more positive, and the atom at the head becomes one unit more negative.

axioms.title: Charge that is spread out, or sits on an atom that can bear it, is lower in energy
axioms.statement: An ion is more stable when its charge is shared by resonance, pulled on by induction, held on a larger atom, on a more electronegative atom, or in an orbital with more s character, or when it completes an aromatic ring. The more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the acid.
axioms.why: Acid strength, leaving group ability and carbocation stability are all this one idea applied to different ions.
explains: Ranking acids (lecture 10/29 and the exam's ranking question): compare the conjugate bases, factor by factor.
Leaving groups (lecture 11/05): a good leaving group is a stable anion, the conjugate base of a strong acid, so {{I-}} and tosylate leave and {{F-}} and {{HO-}} do not.
Carbocations in SN1 and E1 (lecture 11/10): more alkyl groups, or resonance, spread the positive charge.
Organometallics (lecture 11/03): a carbanion is a charge on an atom that bears it badly, so RLi and RMgX are very strong bases.
Hybridization (lecture 10/29): ethyne ({{pKa}} 25) is far more acidic than ethane ({{pKa}} 60) because an {{sp}} orbital holds the pair closer to the nucleus.
axioms.refresher:
A concentrated charge costs energy. Anything that spreads it, or puts it on an atom better able to carry it, lowers the energy of the ion. To compare two acids, remove the proton from each and ask which conjugate base is more stable. That one belongs to the stronger acid.

[[mol:CC(=O)[O-]]]

In acetate the negative charge is shared by two oxygens through resonance. In ethoxide it sits on one oxygen. So acetic acid ({{pKa}} 4) is far stronger than ethanol ({{pKa}} about 16).

The factors, with the lecture's examples:

  • Electronegativity (same row): {{H2O}} is a stronger acid than {{NH3}}, which is stronger than {{CH4}}.
  • Size (same column): a larger atom spreads the charge over more space. HI is stronger than HF, and {{H2S}} is stronger than {{H2O}}.
  • Resonance: acetic acid against ethanol.
  • Induction: nearby electronegative atoms pull charge through the bonds. {{CF3CO2H}} ({{pKa}} −1.5) against {{CH3CO2H}} (4).
  • Hybridization: more s character holds the pair closer to the nucleus, so {{sp}} beats {{sp2}} beats {{sp3}}.
  • Aromaticity: an ion that completes a ring of six π electrons is unusually stable.

The same reasoning works for positive charge: a cation is more stable when its charge is shared.

axioms.title: Acid-base equilibria run toward the weaker acid and the weaker base
axioms.statement: A proton transfer favours the side with the weaker acid (the higher {{pKa}}) and the weaker base. {{pKa}} is a logarithmic scale, so the equilibrium constant is ten to the power of the difference: {{Keq}} = 10<sup>(pKa of product acid − pKa of reactant acid)</sup>.
axioms.why: It turns a table of about fifteen numbers into a prediction for any proton transfer, with a size.
explains: The exam's equilibrium question (lecture 10/29): say which side is favoured and estimate {{Keq}} from two {{pKa}} values.
Organometallics (lecture 11/03): RLi and RMgX are destroyed by water or alcohols because the alkane formed ({{pKa}} 50 to 60) is a far weaker acid than water (15.7).
Choosing a mechanism (the flowchart): a strong base is the conjugate base of a weak acid, and strong bases push toward E2.
Leaving groups (lecture 11/05): the lower the {{pKa}} of H-LG, the better the leaving group.
Making an alkoxide or an acetylide (lectures 10/29 and 11/03): pick a base whose conjugate acid has a higher {{pKa}} than the acid you want to deprotonate.
axioms.refresher:
{{pKa}} = −log {{Ka}}. A low {{pKa}} means a strong acid. Each unit is a factor of ten: an acid of {{pKa}} 4 is a million times stronger than one of {{pKa}} 10.

In a proton transfer there is an acid on each side: the one that gives the proton, and the one that is formed (the conjugate acid of the base). The strong acid gives its proton away more willingly, so the mixture ends up mostly as the weaker acid and the weaker base.

[[eqr:O + [NH2-]>>[OH-] + N]]

Water has {{pKa}} 15.7. Ammonia, the acid on the right, has {{pKa}} 38. Ammonia is the weaker acid, so the equilibrium lies to the right.

How far: {{Keq}} = 10(38 − 15.7) = 1022.3. For practical purposes the reaction is complete.

The method, every time:

  1. Find the acid on the left and the acid on the right.
  2. Look up the two {{pKa}} values.
  3. The side with the higher {{pKa}} is favoured.
  4. {{Keq}} = 10 to the power (product acid {{pKa}} − reactant acid {{pKa}}). If the exponent is negative, the reaction lies to the left.

A stronger acid always has the weaker conjugate base, so the two rules never disagree.

axioms.title: Free energy sets the position of an equilibrium
axioms.statement: {{dG}}° = −RT ln {{Keq}}. At 25 °C every factor of ten in {{Keq}} is worth about 1.36 kcal/mol, and the lower side is the favoured side.
axioms.why: It converts between the two languages the unit uses, energies in kcal/mol and ratios of molecules.
explains: Chairs (lecture 10/27): the energy gap between two chairs, from the A-values, gives the ratio of the two at equilibrium.
Ring strain (lectures 10/20 and 10/27): heats of formation per {{CH2}} compare how much energy each ring holds.
Acid-base equilibria (lecture 10/29): a difference of one {{pKa}} unit is the same 1.36 kcal/mol.
Energy diagrams (lectures 11/05 and 11/10): the height of the products against the reactants is {{dG}}°, and it says how far the reaction goes, not how fast.
Butane conformations (lecture 10/20): a gauche form 0.9 kcal/mol above anti is still a large share of the mixture.
axioms.refresher:
Free energy ({{dG}}) is the quantity that decides where an equilibrium settles. If the products are lower in free energy than the reactants, {{dG}}° is negative and the products are favoured.

The link is {{dG}}° = −RT ln {{Keq}}. At 25 °C, RT is 0.592 kcal/mol, and since ln 10 is 2.303 this becomes

{{dG}}° = −1.36 × log {{Keq}} (kcal/mol, at 25 °C).

So each factor of ten in the ratio costs 1.36 kcal/mol:

  • {{dG}}° = 0: {{Keq}} = 1, a 50 to 50 mixture.
  • {{dG}}° = −1.36: {{Keq}} = 10, about 91 to 9.
  • {{dG}}° = −2.72: {{Keq}} = 100, about 99 to 1.
  • {{dG}}° = −4.08: {{Keq}} = 1000.
[[energy:R=0,TS=15,P=-3]]

On an energy diagram {{dG}}° is the difference in height between the two ends. In this picture the products lie 3 kcal/mol lower, so {{Keq}} = 10(3 / 1.36), about 160. The height of the peak in the middle plays no part in that number.

Small energies matter. A difference of only 1 kcal/mol already gives a ratio of about 5 to 1. That is why a single axial methyl group is enough to decide which chair a molecule prefers.

axioms.title: The rate is set by the highest barrier, not by ΔG
axioms.statement: On an energy diagram intermediates are valleys and transition states are peaks. The rate depends on the height of the highest peak above the reactants ({{Ea}}), and the rate law contains only the species that take part up to and including that rate-determining step.
axioms.why: It is how a rate law tells you the mechanism, and how a mechanism tells you what will speed a reaction up.
explains: SN2 (lecture 11/05): one step with both partners in it, so rate = k[Nu][R-LG].
SN1 and E1 (lecture 11/10): the slow step is ionization, so rate = k[R-LG] and the nucleophile's concentration does not matter.
E2 (lecture 11/12): one step with base and substrate, so rate = k[base][R-LG].
The exam's energy diagram question: count the steps, mark each intermediate and transition state, and say which step is rate-determining.
The exam's 'which reaction is faster' pairs: compare barriers, not the stability of the products.
axioms.refresher:
An energy diagram plots energy against the progress of a reaction. Two different things can be read from it.

  • How far the reaction goes: the height of the products against the reactants, {{dG}}°.
  • How fast it goes: the height of the highest peak above the reactants, the activation energy {{Ea}}. A higher barrier means a slower reaction.

These are independent. A strongly downhill reaction can be very slow.

[[energy:R=0,TS1=22,I=12,TS2=15,P=-6|I=intermediate,TS1=rate-determining]]

A transition state is a peak. It has partly formed and partly broken bonds, lasts for no time at all, and cannot be isolated. An intermediate is a valley between two peaks: a real species with full bonds, such as a carbocation, even if it is short-lived. The number of peaks is the number of steps.

The step that crosses the highest peak is the rate-determining step. Here it is step 1.

The rate law lists what has to come together to get over that peak. If the slow step involves only the substrate, the rate is k[substrate], and adding more of a reagent that enters later changes nothing. If the slow step needs two species, both concentrations appear.

axioms.title: A transition state resembles the species nearest to it in energy
axioms.statement: Hammond's postulate: in an uphill step the transition state is late and looks like the product of that step, and in a downhill step it is early and looks like the reactant. Whatever stabilizes the species it resembles also lowers the barrier.
axioms.why: Transition states cannot be observed, so this is how the stability of something you can draw predicts a rate.
explains: SN1 and E1 (lecture 11/10): ionization is uphill, the transition state looks like the carbocation, so a more stable carbocation forms faster.
The exam's 'which substrate reacts fastest' question for SN1: rank the carbocations and you have ranked the rates.
Zaitsev's rule (lecture 11/12): the transition state of an elimination already looks partly like the alkene, so the more stable alkene usually forms faster.
The exam's transition state drawing question: partial bonds and partial charges are placed according to which side the transition state resembles.
Rearrangements (lecture 11/10): a shift that gives a more stable cation is downhill and has a low barrier.
axioms.refresher:
A transition state exists for an instant, so nobody can look at one. Hammond's postulate says what it must be like: it resembles whichever stable species lies closest to it in energy.

[[energy:R=0,TS=20,P=17]]

This step is uphill. The peak (20) is close in energy to the product (17) and far from the reactant (0). So the transition state is late: bonds are almost fully broken or formed, and its structure is close to the product's.

In a downhill step the opposite holds. The peak is near the reactant, the transition state is early, and it looks like the reactant.

Why this is useful: if the transition state looks like the product of the step, then anything that stabilizes that product stabilizes the transition state too. The barrier drops and the step speeds up.

The standard case is a leaving group departing to give a carbocation. The step is uphill, so the transition state looks like the carbocation, with most of the positive charge already on carbon. A substrate that gives a more stable carbocation therefore ionizes faster. That is the whole reason carbocation stability can be used to rank rates.

Be careful with the direction of the argument. Product stability predicts rate only when the transition state resembles the product.

axioms.title: Tetrahedral carbon wants 109.5°, staggered beats eclipsed, and crowding costs energy
axioms.statement: An {{sp3}} carbon is lowest in energy with bond angles of 109.5° and with the bonds on neighbouring carbons staggered. Squeezed angles (angle strain), eclipsed bonds (torsional strain) and groups pushed together (steric strain, 0.9 kcal/mol for a gauche pair of methyl groups) all raise the energy.
axioms.why: Ring strain, the chair and every A-value are these three costs added up.
explains: Cyclopropane and cyclobutane (lecture 10/20): 60° and about 90° angles, with eclipsed C-H bonds, make small rings strained.
The chair (lectures 10/20 and 10/27): it is the one cyclohexane shape with no angle strain and every bond staggered.
Axial substituents (lecture 10/27): an axial methyl group is gauche to two ring bonds, which is where its cost comes from.
The exam's 'draw both chairs and choose' question: add up the costs of the axial groups in each chair.
SN2 rates (lecture 11/10): crowding around the carbon raises the energy of the transition state, so methyl is fastest and tertiary does not react.
axioms.refresher:
A carbon with four single bonds is {{sp3}} and its bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. There are three ways to make such a carbon unhappy.

Angle strain. Force the angle away from 109.5° and the energy rises. Cyclopropane's ring angles are 60°.

Torsional strain. Look down a C-C bond (a Newman projection). The bonds on the front carbon can sit between those on the back carbon (staggered) or directly in front of them (eclipsed). Eclipsed is higher in energy: in ethane by about 3 kcal/mol.

Steric strain. Two groups pushed into the same space repel each other.

Butane, looking down the middle bond, shows all of this. With the two methyl groups opposite each other (anti, 180° apart) nothing is crowded:

[[newman:CH3,H,H|H,CH3,H|60]]

Turn the back carbon so that the methyl groups are 60° apart (gauche). The shape is still staggered, but the methyl groups touch, and that costs 0.9 kcal/mol:

[[newman:CH3,H,H|CH3,H,H|60]]

The worst shape has the two methyl groups eclipsed.

Keep the 0.9 in mind. An axial methyl group on a cyclohexane has two of these gauche interactions with the ring, and the cost of an axial group is counted in exactly this way.

axioms.title: Wedges, dashes and the kinds of stereoisomer
axioms.statement: A wedge points toward you and a dash points away. A carbon with four different groups is a chirality centre. Stereoisomers that are mirror images that cannot be superimposed are enantiomers, and stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers.
axioms.why: The exam asks what happens to a chirality centre in each mechanism, and whether two chairs or two products are the same compound.
explains: SN2 (lecture 11/05): the configuration at the carbon inverts, so a wedge becomes a dash.
SN1 (lecture 11/10): attack on either face of the planar carbocation gives both enantiomers, a racemic mixture.
Cis and trans rings (lecture 10/27): cis and trans isomers of a disubstituted cyclohexane are diastereomers, and up or down on the flat ring is the wedge or dash.
The exam's chair relationship question: decide whether two chairs are the same molecule, enantiomers or diastereomers.
E2 (lecture 11/12): which alkene forms depends on the three-dimensional arrangement of H and the leaving group.
axioms.refresher:
A flat drawing needs a way to show depth. A plain line lies in the page. A solid wedge comes out toward you. A dashed bond goes back, away from you.

[[mol:C[C@H](Cl)CC]]

The carbon holding Cl has four different groups: Cl, {{CH3}}, {{CH2CH3}} and H (not drawn). That makes it a chirality centre. Swap any two of its groups, or turn the wedge into a dash, and you get a different molecule:

[[mol:C[C@@H](Cl)CC]]

These two are mirror images that cannot be laid on top of each other. They are enantiomers. Enantiomers have the same energy and the same properties, except toward other chiral things. The labels R and S name the two arrangements.

With two or more chirality centres there are more possibilities:

  • Every centre opposite (R,R against S,S): enantiomers.
  • Some centres the same and some opposite (R,R against R,S): diastereomers. These are different compounds with different energies and properties.

A molecule with a mirror plane inside it is achiral, even if it has chirality centres, and is identical to its mirror image.

A carbon with two identical groups is never a chirality centre. Check for that first: it saves the most time.

axioms.title: Orbitals must line up for a reaction to happen
axioms.statement: New bonds form where a filled orbital can overlap an empty one, so geometry is part of every mechanism: a nucleophile attacks a C-LG bond from the side opposite the leaving group, an E2 needs H and the leaving group anti-periplanar (180° apart), and a carbocation is {{sp2}}, flat, with an empty p orbital open on both faces.
axioms.why: It explains the stereochemistry of every mechanism in the unit instead of leaving four rules to memorize.
explains: SN2 inversion (lecture 11/05): backside attack turns the carbon inside out like an umbrella in the wind.
SN1 racemization (lecture 11/10): the flat carbocation can be attacked from the top or the bottom.
E2 on a cyclohexane (lecture 11/12 and the exam's ring E2 question): H and the leaving group are anti-periplanar only when both are axial.
E2 stereochemistry (lecture 11/12): the anti arrangement fixes which alkene isomer forms.
SN2 and crowding (lecture 11/10): groups on the carbon block the one direction of approach that works.
axioms.refresher:
A bond forms when a filled orbital on one atom overlaps an empty orbital on another. Orbitals point in definite directions, so a reaction only works from certain angles.

Attack from the back. The empty orbital of a C-Br bond (its antibonding orbital) is largest on carbon, on the side pointing away from bromine. A nucleophile has to arrive there, 180° from the leaving group. The three other groups on carbon flip to the other side as it comes in.

Anti-periplanar. When a base removes a hydrogen and a leaving group departs in one step, the electrons of the C-H bond flow into the back of the C-LG bond. For that, H and LG must lie in one plane on opposite sides of the C-C bond, a dihedral angle of 180°:

[[newman:Br,H,H|CH3,H,H|60]]

In this Newman projection the back hydrogen pointing straight down is anti to Br. The back {{CH3}} and the other back hydrogen are gauche to it, 60° away.

Flat cations. A carbon with only three bonds and a positive charge is {{sp2}}: three bonds in a plane at 120°, and an empty p orbital sticking out above and below.

[[mol:C[C+](C)C]]

A nucleophile can add to either lobe, so both faces are open.

axioms.title: Carbocation stability, and rearrangement to a more stable cation
axioms.statement: Carbocation stability runs tertiary, then secondary, then primary, then methyl, because alkyl groups donate electron density to the empty p orbital. Allylic and benzylic cations are stabilized by resonance. A carbocation will rearrange by a 1,2 shift of H or of an alkyl group if that gives a more stable cation.
axioms.why: It decides whether SN1 and E1 can happen at all, how fast, and whether the carbon skeleton changes on the way.
explains: SN1 and E1 (lecture 11/10): tertiary substrates ionize, and methyl and ordinary primary ones never do.
The decision flowchart: 'methyl or primary' rules out SN1 and E1, except for allylic and benzylic carbons.
Rearrangements (lecture 11/10 and the exam's rearrangement mechanism): a secondary cation next to a more substituted carbon shifts a hydride or a methyl group.
The exam's 'which reacts fastest by SN1' question: rank the carbocations.
SN1 products (lecture 11/10): when a product has the nucleophile on a carbon that never held the leaving group, a shift happened.
axioms.refresher:
A carbocation has only six electrons around carbon, so it is very electron poor. Anything that feeds electron density to the empty p orbital stabilizes it.

Alkyl groups help. The C-H and C-C bonds next to the positive carbon overlap with the empty p orbital and share their electrons with it (hyperconjugation). More alkyl groups means more sharing:

tertiary (three alkyl groups) is more stable than secondary (two), which is more stable than primary (one), which is more stable than methyl (none).

[[mol:C[C+](C)C]]

Resonance helps more. When the positive carbon is next to a double bond (allylic) or a benzene ring (benzylic), the charge is shared between two or more carbons:

[[mol:C=C[CH2+]]]

A primary allylic or benzylic cation is about as stable as a secondary or tertiary one. Methyl and ordinary primary cations are too unstable to form in solution.

Rearrangement. If a neighbouring carbon holds a hydrogen or an alkyl group whose move would give a better cation, it moves, taking its bonding pair along (a 1,2 shift):

[[rxn:CC(C)[CH+]C>>C[C+](C)CC]]

Here a hydrogen moves with its two electrons from the neighbouring carbon to the positive carbon. A secondary cation becomes a tertiary one. Whenever you draw a carbocation, look at its neighbours before going on.

axioms.title: Solvents stabilize ions, and protic solvents stabilize anions most
axioms.statement: A polar protic solvent has an O-H or N-H bond and stabilizes ions by hydrogen bonding, anions most of all. A polar aprotic solvent is polar but has no O-H or N-H, so it solvates cations and leaves anions bare and reactive.
axioms.why: The same substrate and nucleophile can follow different mechanisms in different solvents, and the flowchart asks about the solvent.
explains: SN2 (lecture 11/05): a polar aprotic solvent leaves the nucleophile unsolvated, so SN2 is much faster in it.
SN1 and E1 (lecture 11/10): a polar protic solvent stabilizes the carbocation and the leaving group as they form, so ionization is faster in it.
Nucleophile strength (lecture 11/05 and the exam's 'better nucleophile' pairs): in a protic solvent small anions are held tightly by hydrogen bonds and react more slowly.
The decision flowchart: for a secondary carbon the first question is whether the solvent is polar protic.
Acidity in solution (lecture 10/29): how well the solvent can reach an anion changes its stability, which is why the {{pKa}} values of the small alcohols differ.
axioms.refresher:
Ions are high in energy on their own. In solution, solvent molecules gather around them and lower that energy. This is solvation, and how well it works depends on the solvent.

Polar protic solvents have a hydrogen on O or N: water, methanol, ethanol, acetic acid.

[[mol:CO]]

The δ+ hydrogen of the O-H group forms hydrogen bonds to anions, and the oxygen lone pairs surround cations. Both kinds of ion are stabilized, and anions especially. A small anion with concentrated charge, such as {{F-}}, is held tightly inside a cage of solvent and has to shed it before it can react.

Polar aprotic solvents are polar but have no O-H or N-H: acetone, DMSO, DMF, acetonitrile.

[[mol:CS(C)=O]]

DMSO has hydrogens, but they are on carbon and cannot hydrogen bond. Its oxygen still solvates cations well. Anions are left almost bare, so they are much more reactive.

Two consequences to carry into the unit:

  • A reaction that makes ions from a neutral molecule is helped by a polar protic solvent.
  • A reaction that needs a reactive anion is helped by a polar aprotic solvent.

To classify a solvent, look for a hydrogen on oxygen or nitrogen. Nothing else makes it protic.
